Thanks for providing the methylKit R package. I think it is one of the most useful program for methylation study.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Regards,

Jongbum Kim.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jong,

MethylKit has multiple annotation functions:
annotate.WithFeature()
annotate.WithFeature.Flank()
annotate.WithGenicParts()
Each of the above performs annotation however to a unique subject. For eg., annotate.WithFeature.Flank() could be used to annotate CpG Islands and shoresl; annotate.WithGenicParts() could be used to annotate genic elements like promoter, introns, exons.

In order to perform annotations, one has to create the subject (ie., CpG islands/shore or genic elements). MethylKit offers functions to create them also.

One can get very good information about creating and using the annotation objects by following the vignette from the methylKit website <https://code.google.com/p/methylkit/>. MethylKit provides very good coersion function that will help you to achieve the kind of table you wanted (Its not straight forward but possible with some knowledge of R/bioconductor and basic linux shell scripting)

Here is a blog post <http://chitka-kalyan.blogspot.fi/2014/10/extending-methylkit-extract-promoters.html> that may help you reach your goal. I would probably do the following for the kind of table you wanted:
Create annotation object from refseq/ENSEMBL annotation using read.transcript.features()
Get the DMR object (I am assuming that it will be a methylDiff object) and coerce it into GRanges using as()
Find intersecting/overlapping ranges  between DMR and each genic region (promoter/exon/intron)
For each intersecting ranges name an additional column that identifies the genic elements. Eg., label a metacolumn as 'promoter' for the promoter overlapping ranges
combine all the labelled and overlapping ranges into one object eg., c(promoter_DMRs, exon_DMRs........)
Export the ranges into a bed file/table
Pls note that the above instructions/functions may not work out of the box. It depends on the kind of the objects one starts with. But I hope this may give you a direction to start with and achieve your table!

Regards,
Kalyan

messages.body_plain:
The problem here is the underscore "_" in chromosome names, by default read.transcript.features() removes the chromosome names with "_". There are a bunch of such chromosome in human and mouse genome and possibly other genomes, normally we do not work on those chromosomes although they are part of the assembly. setting remove.unsual=FALSE when calling the function should resolve the issue.

Best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
you have low coverage samples and there is also and error message about the SAM file format, make sure the format of the files resembles the ones in the examples in the package
https://code.google.com/p/methylkit/source/browse/inst/extdata/test.fastq_bismark.sorted.min.sam

it is not easy to suggest a solution where we can't replicate the problem. You need to find out on your own by trial and error what files are giving the error, and if the error relates to file format or low coverage. General suggestions are that the data is low coverage and bases are either filtered on coverage or quality thresholds and the program exits without being able calculate conversion rate. The second error suggests a file format issue, make sure the file format is correct.

The last solution I can suggest is to use Bismark scripts to output a per base methylation information including coverage and methylation ratios. There are some scripts in the latest bismark that can do that, and try to format and read that file into methylKit.

Best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
I would also suggest you check base qualities from your samples. If they are systematically low, it indicates a problem with your samples.

For your question you need to process the files you get from Bismark to a format that is acceptable by methylKit. Please see the blog posts on this:
http://zvfak.blogspot.de/2012/10/how-to-read-bsmap-methylation-ratio.html
http://zvfak.blogspot.de/2013/03/using-encode-methylation-data-rrbs-in-r.html

The minimal information needed is as follows:
chr,start,end,strand,coverage and ratio of methylation

Example of such a file would be something like this

chr1 12323 - 10 0.1
chr1 22423 + 90 0.76
chr1 32333 + 200 0.83

and this is how you would read the file:
library(methylKit)
obj = read("example.file.txt",
                 sample.id <http://sample.id> = "test", assembly = "hg19", header = FALSE,
                 context = "CpG", resolution = "base",
                 pipeline = list(fraction = TRUE, chr.col = 1, start.col = 2,
                                  end.col = 2,coverage.col = 4, strand.col = 3,
                                  freqC.col = 5))

you have to select for CG context and do some arithmetics on the columns of the "Genome wide cytosin report" to get percent/ratio of methylation and coverage values.
This doable via a small perl script or maybe even awk one liner. If you know your way around some scripting language this shouldn't take more than 10 minutes to write.

Best,
Altuna

some update on this:
Cytosine report seems to have uncovered positions as well. And the other files do not have strand information so they can not be imported to methylKit at all.

Even if I write something to import from cytosine report it will take too much time to read all the non-covered bases and filter them out later in R. The best is that user process them beforehand. While the user is processing the files to remove uncovered bases, it is trivial to also process the files to a format acceptable by methylKit. The following awk one-liner will do that, and convert the cytosine report from CpGs to a format readable by methylKit (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/methylkit_discussion/nOk2hM439Ak/5HBB5jefadYJ)

awk  '{OFS="\t";if($4+0 > 0 || $5+0 >0 ) print $1,$2,$3,$4/($4+$5),$4+$5;}' cytosineReport.txt > outputForMethylKit

this will give chr,start,strand, methylationRatio,coverage

>
> Given the small differentially methylation difference between the treated and control group, the p and q value looks a little suspicious as I expect a little more variation between groups.
>
> My questions are:
> (1) Is it normal to have a p and q value of zero?

They are probably not exactly zero but very very small, but it gets output as 0.

> (2) How is regional analysis calculated? My current understanding is that the counts for Cs (methylated) and Ts (unmethylated) are summed across regions and a logistic regression is performed between stress and control groups. Is my understanding of it correct?
>

Correct, if there are replicates. if not, it does fisher's exact test. you probably have lots of counts, that increases the power of detecting small differences. For simplicity, I will give an example of comparing frequencies with fisher's exact test, in this case having more counts gives you more confidence to discriminate small differences.
The following frequency tables represent numCs and numTs for a test and control case, the percent methylations are the same in both cases however the table with larger counts have a lower P-value.

fisher.test(matrix(c(10,10,15,10),nrow=2))
odds ratio=~ 0.67   P-value= 0.5572

fisher.test(matrix(c(100,100,150,100),nrow=2))
odds ratio=~ 0.67   P-value= 0.03611
